name: Dry fasting
lead: Dry fasting is abstaining from both food and fluids for a period of time. It is the form of fasting used in Ramadan, the Bahá'í nineteen-day fast and some Lenten and Yom Kippur observances, where the fast is limited to daylight hours or about a day, and it is also promoted in some wellness and body-composition circles as a longer, stricter version of water fasting.[1][14][15][2]

People who try it for their appearance are usually after leanness: fasting lowers calorie intake and body weight, and advocates in online communities say stricter fasting deepens effects such as autophagy, the cell-recycling process.[3][13][17] Studies of dawn-to-dusk dry fasting report weight and body-mass-index reductions, while a review of fasting notes that in early prolonged fasting about two-thirds of weight lost is reported to be lean muscle and that weight lost during Ramadan is often regained within about two weeks.[1][3][15]

Research on dry fasting is small and mostly examines religious daytime fasts in healthy volunteers, plus one small five-day study of physiology in ten participants.[2][3][4][6][10] Medical sources note that prolonged fasting can cause electrolyte losses, and abstaining from fluids adds a dehydration risk.[1][16]

Fasting: voluntary abstinence from foods or foods and beverages; prolonged fasting is 4 or more consecutive days[9]
Hydration, glucose, circadian phase, body weight, inflammation, gingival health[2][3][12]

paras: Fasting broadly means voluntarily abstaining from food and sometimes drink.[1] An international Delphi consensus on fasting terminology, with 38 experts, defined fasting as voluntary abstinence from some or all foods or foods and beverages, and defined short-term fasting as lasting 2 to 3 days and prolonged fasting as 4 or more consecutive days.[9] Many faiths include fasts of this kind: Muslims abstain from food and liquid from dawn to sunset during Ramadan, Jews observe a roughly 25-hour fast on Yom Kippur, and the Bahá'í Faith observes a nineteen-day fast in March.[1][14] Researchers classify daytime fasts like these as forms of intermittent dry fasting.[2][4]
Wellness and body-composition circles use the term more broadly for fasts of a day or longer in which no water is consumed, sometimes after a period of water fasting.[13]

Ramadan fasting is obligatory for Muslims who have reached puberty and runs from dawn to sunset, with a predawn meal (suhur) and a sunset meal (iftar); exemptions include the sick, travelers, the elderly, pregnant or breastfeeding women and children.[14] Wikipedia reports that Ramadan fasting is considered safe for healthy people when overall food and water intake is adequate, that modest weight loss is common, and that weight may return afterward.[14] A study of 55 professional soccer players found declines in speed, agility and endurance during Ramadan.[14]

The Bahá'í fast runs from sunrise to sunset for 19 days in March and has become a study model because it is a month-long daily dry fast practiced by volunteers.[2][11] Historically fasting has also been promoted for health outside religion, such as Upton Sinclair's 1911 book The Fasting Cure, which Wikipedia describes as making sweeping unsupported claims, and Morris Fishbein's 1932 listing of fasting as a fad diet.[1]

On looksmax.org dry fasting appears in a thread titled 'Anyone here dry fasting?', in which the original poster describes plans for a five-day dry fast after two days of water fasting and says autophagy increases an insane amount.[13] A reply from a member who says they dry fasted for eight days describes it as brutal, with difficulty standing, but reports that finger warts shrank, joints felt better for about two weeks, and that it introduced them to autophagy.[13]

Studies of dry fasting measure weight, glucose, hydration and inflammation markers rather than facial or skin appearance, so appearance effects beyond weight are described only by advocates.[3][4][7][8]

sections.h: Claims about autophagy and cell renewal
paras: Autophagy is the cell's process of breaking down and recycling its own components; it was first observed in rat liver cells in 1962, named by Christian de Duve in 1963, and its genetic machinery was identified in yeast in the 1990s, work that earned Yoshinori Ohsumi the 2016 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.[17] Nutrient deprivation is a classic trigger in yeast and cultured cells, and the nutrient-sensing kinases mTOR and AMPK regulate it in mammals.[17]

Wikipedia notes that most mechanistic evidence comes from yeast, mice and cultured cells, and that more autophagy is not automatically beneficial, as it can both protect and kill cells.[17] No study has measured autophagy during dry fasting for appearance outcomes.

A small study of ten participants who dry-fasted for five consecutive days measured hormones daily and described responses to reduced blood volume (hypovolemia) and increased solute concentration (hypertonicity), including ADH, aldosterone and cortisol.[6] A follow-up analysis described three primary risks of dry fasting, hypovolemia, hypertonicity and hypoglycemia, and reported weight and body circumferences falling to minima on day 5, insulin and insulin resistance reaching minima on day 4, and growth hormone, cholesterol and ketone (acetoacetate) levels rising to maxima on day 5.[10]
Dehydration signs from the general medical literature include thirst, headache, reduced urine output, sunken eyes and reduced skin turgor.[16]

In a three-arm randomized trial of 16 subjects without diabetes, Bahá'í dry fasting, 16:8 time-restricted eating and control were compared; only the dry-fasting group reduced caloric intake (about 678 kcal), body weight (about 1.9 kg) and BMI (about 0.65) over 19 days, and the dry-fasting group showed higher maximum glucose values.[3] A cohort of healthy people studied during Ramadan intermittent fasting examined anthropometric, inflammatory and mental-health parameters.[4] Wikipedia's intermittent fasting article reports that most human studies of intermittent fasting find weight loss of 2.5 to 9.9 percent, mainly from fat, with some lean mass lost.[15]

Wikipedia's fasting article reports that in early prolonged fasting about two-thirds of weight lost is lean muscle, and that fasting does not appear to benefit athletic performance in the intermittent fasting literature.[1][15]

Wikipedia notes that prolonged fasting can lead to loss of sodium, potassium and magnesium and may cause low blood sodium, muscle loss, gallstones, and refeeding syndrome after about four to five days without food.[1] A 2026 narrative review summarises fasting effects across several body systems.[5]

Dehydration is described in general medical sources as follows: loss of 1 to 2 percent of body water can impair cognitive performance, 5 to 8 percent causes fatigue and dizziness, and complications include hypernatremia, heatstroke, kidney stones and hypovolemic shock.[16] Medical guidance for fasting generally addresses food abstinence; the effects of complete dry fasting beyond daytime fasts have received little formal study.[1][10] Ramadan exemptions and published concerns for pregnancy and kidney disease are recorded.[14]

A cohort of 34 healthy Bahá'í volunteers was studied during the 19-day daytime dry fast for safety and effects on hydration, metabolism and the circadian clock.[2] A self-controlled cohort of 11 healthy men examined energy expenditure and metabolic parameters during the same fast.[11]

In a small study, ten participants performed dry fasting for five consecutive days with daily monitoring of hormones including ADH, aldosterone and cortisol, to describe the physiological responses to reduced blood volume and increased solute concentration.[6] A companion analysis examined glucose, insulin, growth hormone and thyroid hormones.[10]

A three-arm randomized trial in 16 subjects without diabetes compared Bahá'í dry fasting, time-restricted eating and control on glucose profiles.[3] A 2025 three-arm trial of 66 healthy participants with experimentally induced gingivitis found less increase in gum bleeding in the Bahá'í dry-fasting group than in control or 16:8 time-restricted eating.[12]

A prospective cohort of healthy people examined body composition, inflammatory and mental-health parameters during Ramadan.[4] Dawn-to-dusk dry fasting studies in people with metabolic syndrome or raised body mass index examined inflammatory cytokines and proteome changes.[7][8]

timeline.event: Upton Sinclair publishes The Fasting Cure, popularising fasting as a cure-all.[1]
Physician Morris Fishbein lists fasting among fad diets.[1]
Autophagy is first observed in rat liver cells.[17]
Christian de Duve coins the term autophagy.[17]
Yoshinori Ohsumi wins the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on autophagy.[17]
A study of five-day dry fasting in ten participants describes responses to hypovolemia and hypertonicity.[6]
Studies of the Bahá'í 19-day daytime dry fast report hydration, glucose and circadian effects.[2][11]
Dawn-to-dusk dry fasting study in metabolic syndrome examines blood cell proteome.[7]
Randomized three-arm trial compares dry fasting with time-restricted eating; expert consensus defines fasting terms.[3][9]
Studies report gingival effects of dry fasting and hypoglycemia compensation in a five-day dry fast.[10][12]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org dry fasting is discussed in a handful of threads as a stricter, faster version of water fasting, with autophagy as the main stated reason.[13]

claims.claim: Dry fasting increases autophagy far more than other fasts.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster says it increases autophagy 'an insane amount' and a reply says it got them onto the autophagy wagon.[13]
claims.experts: Autophagy is induced by nutrient deprivation in yeast, mice and cultured cells; human data are limited, and no study has compared autophagy in dry fasting with other fasts.[17]

claims.claim: Dry fasting shrinks warts and eases joint pain.
claims.believers: One forum member says finger warts shrank and joints felt better for about two weeks after an eight-day dry fast.[13]
claims.experts: No published human trial has tested dry fasting for warts or joint pain; the fasting studies examine glucose, hydration, weight and inflammation markers.[2][3][8]

claims.believers: Fasting is widely used for weight loss, and a looksmax.org poster plans a multi-day dry fast alongside water fasting.[13]
claims.experts: A randomized trial found weight loss of about 1.9 kg over 19 days of Bahá'í daytime fasting [3]; Wikipedia reports two-thirds of early prolonged-fasting weight loss is lean mass and Ramadan weight is often regained within two weeks.[1][15]

claims.believers: Some members and fasting advocates list reduced inflammation among the effects they look for from fasting.[13]
claims.experts: Studies of dawn-to-dusk dry fasting in people with metabolic syndrome or raised BMI report lower inflammatory cytokines and altered proteome profiles.[7][8]

claims.believers: A poster plans a five-day dry fast after two days of water fasting, and another says they completed eight days.[13]
claims.experts: Research covers daytime fasts and a five-day study in ten participants, with hypovolemia, hypertonicity and hypoglycemia identified as primary risks.[2][6][10] Dehydration and electrolyte loss are documented risks.[1][16]

card.summary: No food and no water; research covers religious daytime fasts, while longer dry fasts carry dehydration risk.
card.note: Complete fluid abstinence beyond daytime fasting is little studied and associated with dehydration risk.

quick.overview:
Dry fasting means going without both food and water. Studies cover religious daytime fasts such as Ramadan and the Bahá'í fast, plus one small five-day physiology study.

Online advocates cite autophagy and other benefits; these claims have not been tested for appearance.
quick.mechanism: Without fluids the body faces reduced blood volume and higher solute concentration, triggering hormones such as vasopressin and aldosterone.
quick.risks: Prolonged fasting can cause electrolyte losses and, without fluids, dehydration. Long dry fasts have little formal safety research.

chain: Food and fluids are withheld for a set period
Calorie intake and body weight fall during the fast
Advocates expect a leaner look, with claims of autophagy and other effects
angle.text: People use dry fasting, from daytime religious fasts to multi-day versions, to lower weight and aim for a leaner look. Studies of daytime fasts report modest weight loss; claims of effects beyond weight are advocates' descriptions.
